title: The contrary view, that immortality was man's natural condition, was condemned by Pius V and Gregory XIII
source_text: XII. Fuerunt quidem nonnulli superiore saeculo, inter ipsos Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, qui existimaverunt immortalitatem primi hominis non fuisse gratiae beneficium, sed naturalem ejus conditionem. Verum haec sententia fuit a Pontificibus Romanis Pio V. & Gregorio XIII. damnata in bulla singulari, in qua multos articulos recentiorum quorundam Theologorum damnaverunt. Inter quos articulos hic est 75. Immortalitas primi hominis non erat gratiae beneficium, sed naturalis ejus conditio. Ut testatur idem Bellarm. lib. de Grat. primi hominis.
pass_a_gloss: There were indeed some in the former century, among the Doctors of the Roman Church themselves, who thought that the immortality of the first man was not a benefit of grace, but his natural condition. But this opinion was condemned by the Roman Pontiffs Pius V and Gregory XIII in a particular bull, in which they condemned many articles of certain more recent Theologians. Among which articles this is the 75th. The immortality of the first man was not a benefit of grace, but his natural condition. As the same Bellarmine testifies, book on the Grace of the first man.
pass_b_english: In the last century there were indeed some among the teachers of the Roman Church itself who held that the first man's immortality was not a gift of grace but his natural condition.

But the Roman popes Pius V and Gregory XIII condemned this view in a special bull in which they condemned many articles of certain recent theologians. Article 75 among them reads: "The immortality of the first man was not a gift of grace, but his natural condition." So Bellarmine himself testifies (On the Grace of the First Man).

choices.why: Singularis here means a particular, separate bull, not an extraordinary one.
